# Walk-forward coin ranking by total equity and tail risk

# Walk-forward coin ranking by total equity and tail risk — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Walk-forward coin ranking by total equity and tail risk. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-08 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] Bailey and coauthors state that their PBO procedure does not check whether a backtest has correct transaction costs or uses only data available at the decision time. They also warn that it can miss overfitting to a regime when the available dataset contains no structural break outside that regime. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] In their 32-series portfolio example, Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin explain that randomly shuffling individual daily returns destroys autocorrelation. They instead use blocks of returns and the same block starting points across series to preserve the cross-market correlation structure. Their example does not supply a universal block length for crypto bot equity. (low confidence) — https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chekhlov/ChekhlovUryasevZabarankin--03-2004.pdf

## How it works

- [statement] Bailey and coauthors explain that testing many configurations on the same historical data increases the probability of finding false positives. A significance level for one test does not control the selection process across many tests. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] Bailey and coauthors describe overfitting as the case in which the configuration with maximum in-sample performance systematically underperforms other configurations out of sample because it has fitted training noise. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] Bailey and coauthors explicitly warn against using PBO as the objective function for selecting an optimal strategy. They present CSCV as an assessment of the strategy-selection process and call using it to guide the optimal-strategy search a misuse. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Quantpedia's grid examples show that a strategy can have losing days when price trends within the day instead of oscillating. Its comparison is an illustrative currency-grid study, rather than evidence ranking present-day crypto coins. (low confidence) — https://quantpedia.com/a-primer-on-grid-trading-strategy/
- [statement] Freqtrade documents a per-pair profit-to-drawdown objective that returns the worst pair's result so that strong pairs do not conceal weak pairs. This documents an available objective, rather than evidence that it improves a grid or DCA coin-ranking strategy. (low confidence) — https://www.freqtrade.io/en/stable/hyperopt/
- [statement] Freqtrade documents Calmar and profit-versus-drawdown optimization objectives. Their availability shows that maximizing profit and controlling drawdown are distinct configurable objectives; it does not determine the best weights for a candidate-coin ranking. (low confidence) — https://www.freqtrade.io/en/stable/hyperopt/
- [statement] Freqtrade's documentation warns that increasing optimization precision beyond its default three decimal places will usually produce overfitted results. This is a tool-specific warning about search complexity, rather than a universal parameter-precision rule. (low confidence) — https://www.freqtrade.io/en/stable/hyperopt/
- [statement] Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin argue that optimization using maximum drawdown may have significant statistical error because the decision rests on one observation of maximal loss. This is their stated limitation of the criterion, rather than a measured uncertainty interval for crypto grid/DCA rankings. (low confidence) — https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chekhlov/ChekhlovUryasevZabarankin--03-2004.pdf
- [statement] The pinned Frontiers crypto-microstructure study states that it standardizes test features with training-set statistics, right-aligns rolling features so they exclude the forecast interval, and applies its purged walk-forward scheme to hyperparameter tuning and stability selection. These are reported leakage controls for that study, rather than validation of a grid/DCA rolling asset-selection rule. (low confidence) — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/blockchain/articles/10.3389/fbloc.2026.1811716/full
- [statement] In its five-minute long/short experiment aggregated over twelve crypto asset-venue pairs, the pinned Frontiers study reports that all net Sharpe ratios are deeply negative after its Binance VIP-0 fee and slippage assumptions. The authors describe the result as diagnostic rather than prescriptive. This is a negative result for that short-horizon experiment and does not show that grid/DCA ranking fails or succeeds. (low confidence) — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/blockchain/articles/10.3389/fbloc.2026.1811716/full
- [statement] Vanguard explicitly distinguishes investing a lump sum that is available immediately from investing a fixed amount from each paycheck. In its historical lump-sum versus cost-averaging comparison, the base illustration assumes no interest on uninvested cash; its cash-interest sensitivity says that higher cash interest reduces the lump-sum advantage, all else equal. These are benchmark assumptions in a stock/bond study and do not establish a crypto coin-ranking advantage. (low confidence) — https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/cost_averaging_invest_now_or_temporarily_hold_your_cash.pdf
- [statement] Bailey and coauthors describe a partition-size trade-off in CSCV: too few partitions underrepresent the left tail of the logit distribution, while too many can break relevant temporal and seasonal structure across partitions. This is a property of their validation construction, rather than an established training-window or rebalance rule for crypto grid/DCA selection. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] Vanguard illustrates lump-sum versus cost-averaging outcomes using a common initial wealth of $100,000 and a one-year evaluation horizon, with the cost-averaging investment split into three equal monthly parts. These are explicit assumptions of a stock/bond allocation comparison, rather than a crypto coin-selection result. (low confidence) — https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/cost_averaging_invest_now_or_temporarily_hold_your_cash.pdf

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Bailey and coauthors warn that standard holdout techniques can be unreliable in investment backtests and propose combinatorially symmetric cross-validation as a way to estimate probability of backtest overfitting. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] Bailey and coauthors define probability of backtest overfitting as the conditional probability that a strategy selected as optimal in sample underperforms the median out of sample. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] Quantpedia contrasts marking portfolio value through time with reporting only closed trades. In its daily-reset grid example, closed-trade reporting can show only winning trades during the day and hide losses until the remaining inventory closes. (low confidence) — https://quantpedia.com/a-primer-on-grid-trading-strategy/
- [statement] Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin define Conditional Drawdown measures as functionals of a portfolio's drawdown or underwater curve. For a single path and an appropriate tolerance parameter, the drawdown functional is the mean of the worst tail of drawdowns. (low confidence) — https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chekhlov/ChekhlovUryasevZabarankin--03-2004.pdf
- [statement] Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin state that the Conditional Drawdown family includes maximum drawdown and average drawdown as limiting cases. (low confidence) — https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chekhlov/ChekhlovUryasevZabarankin--03-2004.pdf
- [statement] In their CSCV implementation, Bailey and coauthors require synchronous performance observations across candidate configurations and say that configurations trading at different frequencies should be aggregated to a common time index. They also require the selection metric to be estimable on subsamples of each candidate performance series. (low confidence) — https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
- [statement] The Frontiers crypto microstructure study explicitly states that its economic evaluation includes maker/taker fees and half-spread slippage but omits queue-position dynamics, perpetual-futures funding, short-borrow costs, and matching-engine latency. The authors therefore characterize its reported net Sharpe figures as an upper bound for a non-co-located retail-fee participant. (low confidence) — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/blockchain/articles/10.3389/fbloc.2026.1811716/full
- [statement] The abstract of Arian, Norouzi and Seco reports lower backtest-overfitting probability and a better Deflated Sharpe Ratio for CPCV than traditional methods, and reports shortcomings in false-discovery prevention for Walk-Forward. The abstract identifies a synthetic controlled environment with stochastic-volatility, jump-diffusion, drift-burst and regime-switching models. This is an attributed comparison reported in the publisher preview; it does not establish that CPCV universally dominates walk-forward validation for crypto grid/DCA selectors. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950705124011110
